title: the Sri Sukta
hook: a lotus pond drained in summer, all mud, and a hymn that asks the mud itself to bring the goddess home

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta counted riches from the cowshed to the tongue: fragrance at the door, and truth of speech. What true thing did you say? Today, the hymn asks her to stay for good, and a week ends. Day one thousand ninety-nine.

Drain a lotus pond in the dry season and you don't find anything pretty. You find mud. Thick, dark, sour-smelling mud, with old roots running through it like cables. Nobody photographs that part. But that's where the flower lives. Every bloom that floats on the surface in the rains is drawing on what's down there in the dark. The Sri Sukta has been calling the lotus goddess all week. And when it finally asks her to move into the house for good, it doesn't ask the flower to do the inviting. It asks the mud.
screen: `DRAIN THE POND. FIND MUD.` → `THAT'S WHERE THE FLOWER LIVES.` → `THE HYMN ASKS THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. Through Kardama she has children. Kardama, come and dwell with me. Make Sri, the mother garlanded with lotuses, dwell in my family. Kardama is a name, and as a word it means mud. Tradition hears him as her son. So the singer turns to the goddess's own child, the mud, and asks him to move in, so that his mother will follow. Then the next line does the same with water. In paraphrase: may the waters bring forth soft and gentle things. Chiklita, live in my house, and make the divine mother Sri dwell in my family. Chiklita, tradition says, is another of her children, linked to moisture. Mud and water. The two humble things a lotus can't live without. That's a surprising way to ask the goddess of fortune to stay. You might expect the singer to ask the gold, or the elephants, to bring her. Instead he asks the plainest, dampest parts of the earth. And look at the word family. Not my house only, but my line, my people. Some readers hear the ones who come after in that word, and a fortune asked to stay across generations. That's this week, held in one picture. A procession you hear before you see it. A goddess satisfied and satisfying. The turn where her becomes you: I choose you. A bilva tree grown from her own discipline. Alakshmi, shown the door. Fragrance and cow dung and truth of speech. And now mud and water, asked to bring her home. Some readers say the lotus in the mud is the whole hymn: fortune that grows out of ordinary ground. Others keep it plain: a family praying for good seasons. The hymn goes on a little further, calling her once more, but this is where the path leaves it. Tomorrow a different hymn begins, one that praises the goddess by her names.
screen: `KARDAMA, WHOSE NAME MEANS MUD.` · `CHIKLITA, AND THE WATERS.` · `DWELL IN MY FAMILY.` · `A WEEK OF THE SRI SUKTA.` · then, large: `THE LOTUS ASKS THROUGH THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor the mud. Settle, and let the breath slow and sink low, into the belly. Bring to mind something plain and unglamorous that holds your life up. A hard season you came through. A parent's ordinary work. A job nobody thanks you for. The early mornings. Let it be there, without polishing it. Then notice what has grown out of it, something you're glad of now. Rest with the two together, root and flower. If you pray, you can thank the goddess, or God, for both in your own words. If you don't, just let the plain thing be honored for once. The bell holds the time.
The Sri Sukta. The hymn that calls Sri near, chooses her, and finally asks Kardama, the mud, to bring the lotus mother home to stay.
Your line: the Sri Sukta. Today, thank someone for the unglamorous part they play, the mud under your lotus. Day one thousand ninety-nine. A week walked.

howItsDone: Some Hindus chant the whole Sri Sukta at home or in temples during Lakshmi worship, at Diwali and on other days, often while offering lotus flowers, lamps and sweets.

fork.reveal: the hymn asks Kardama, the mud, to dwell with the singer, so that Sri will dwell in the family; then Chiklita and the waters. the lotus is invited through what it grows from.

original.note: Sanskrit: kardama, mud, and in the Sri Sukta a name, heard by tradition as Sri's son.

trapdoor: what you thought: fortune would be invited by the grandest thing in the hymn.
what it means: the hymn asks the mud and the waters, the humble ground of the lotus, to bring Sri home to stay.
what a scholar hears: kardamena prajābhūtā mayi sambhava kardama / śriyaṃ vāsaya me kule mātaraṃ padmamālinīm: Kardama addressed directly, with Sri as the lotus-garlanded mother.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home
the year just walked and kept

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verses 11–12 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)

notes: Verse 11 paraphrased: kardamena prajābhūtā mayi sambhava kardama / śriyaṃ vāsaya me kule mātaraṃ padmamālinīm. Verse 12: āpaḥ sṛjantu snigdhāni ciklīta vasa me gṛhe / ni ca devīṃ mātaraṃ śriyaṃ vāsaya me kule. 'Through Kardama she has children' is a simplification of kardamena prajābhūtā; confirm.
Kardama and Chiklita as Sri's sons, and Chiklita's link to moisture, are traditional readings, attributed to tradition. 'Kardama means mud' is lexical. Confirm.

Week-end look-back for 1093–1099 (procession; satisfied and satisfying; I choose you; the bilva; Alakshmi; cow dung and truth of speech; Kardama). The remaining verses (13–15 and the phalashruti) are not taught; the teach says the hymn goes on a little further.
Last Sri Sukta day; tomorrow begins the Lalita Sahasranama (1100).
Editor pass: 'the hymn asks that she stay across generations' (more than kule, family, says) recast as a 'some readers' reading.
